title: Language and writing
summary: Words for the things words do.

questions.clue: This is a word that means the opposite of another word.
questions.note: Hot and cold are antonyms. A word meaning the same thing is a synonym, and one that sounds the same is a homophone.

questions.clue: This is a shortened form of a word or phrase, such as writing three letters instead of United Nations.
questions.note: An acronym is pronounced as a word, like NATO; an initialism is spelled out, like BBC. Abbreviation covers both.

questions.clue: This is the written account of somebody's life, told by another person.
questions.note: Written by the person themselves it is an autobiography. Bio means life and graphy means writing.

questions.clue: This is the act of presenting somebody else's words or ideas as if they were your own.
questions.note: From the Latin for kidnapper. In an academic context it is treated as misconduct even when it is accidental.

questions.clue: This is a short well-known saying that states a general truth, such as too many cooks spoil the broth.
questions.note: An idiom is different: its meaning cannot be worked out from the words, but it does not state a truth.

questions.clue: This word describes somebody able to speak two languages fluently.
questions.note: Three is trilingual and many is multilingual. Monolingual describes somebody with only one.

questions.clue: This is the original handwritten or typed text of a book before it is published.
questions.note: Literally written by hand, from Latin. Publishers still use the word for a typed document.

questions.clue: This is a section of writing dealing with one idea, beginning on a new line.
questions.note: In an exam essay each one should carry a single point, which is the whole reason the division exists.

questions.clue: This is the list of books and articles an author consulted, printed at the end of a piece of work.
questions.note: A bibliography may list everything read; a reference list contains only what was actually cited.

questions.clue: This is a word or phrase that softens something unpleasant, such as saying passed away instead of died.
questions.note: From Greek words meaning to speak well. The opposite, deliberately making something sound worse, is a dysphemism.
